summary: Describes how FTP reply codes are used in TENEX mail processing, with the aim of more reliable mail service.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 630 explains how TENEX computers use FTP reply codes when mail delivery fails. The code tells a sending process whether the problem is permanent or temporary, so it can stop or try again.

questions: what do ftp error codes 450 to 454 mean
how does tenex handle failed mail delivery
permanent vs temporary mail failure in ftp

subtitle: How TENEX mail systems used FTP reply codes to decide whether to retry delivery.

tldr.problem: Mailing processes could not tell from an FTP error code whether a failed delivery was permanent or worth trying again.
tldr.mechanism: TENEX servers use 450 for permanent user-related failures, 451 for permanent message-related failures and 453 for temporary failures. The mail process treats 452, 453 and 454 as temporary, and 450 and 451 as permanent.
tldr.outcome: This gives TENEX mail senders a clearer rule for retrying delivery. The RFC presents it as an interim use of existing codes while new FTP codes are being designed.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 630's status as Unknown and names no RFC that updates or replaces it. The RFC describes an intended TENEX practice while new FTP error codes were being designed.

sections.title: Why Mail Needs Clear Error Replies
sections.content:
FTP servers already used codes 450 through 454 for failures when carrying out file actions. The same codes applied to mail delivery, but they did not cover every possible cause. Server authors had to assign causes to codes, so a human might learn more from the reply text than a computer process could learn from the code.

TENEX mail senders needed to distinguish permanent failures from temporary ones. For a temporary failure, the process would keep trying to deliver the message for several days.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail program needs to know whether a failed delivery can succeed later. A clear code lets it retry temporary problems and stop on permanent ones.

sections.title: How TENEX Uses the Codes
sections.content:
The TENEX server continues to use codes 452 and 454 for the MLFL command as previously defined. For MAIL and MLFL, it uses 450 for permanent failures caused by the addressed user, such as no mailbox; 451 for permanent failures caused by the message, such as an overlong line; and 453 for temporary failures, such as a busy mailbox or an unexpectedly closed connection.

TENEX mailing processes previously treated every code from 450 to 454 as permanent. Under the planned change, they treat 452, 453 and 454 as temporary, while 450 and 451 remain permanent.
sections.plainLanguage: Code 450 means the addressed user cannot receive the mail, and 451 means the message itself has a permanent problem. Code 453 means a temporary problem, so the sender should try again.

sections.title: Compatibility and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC says this change should not harm mail exchanges between TENEX and non-TENEX sites. The author argues that the new assignments are no further from the original meanings of the codes than the old assignments, and convey more information to mail processes.

The note describes how TENEX sites intend to use the existing codes in the near future. It says new FTP error codes are still being designed.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC expects the new assignments to work with other sites because they are at least as close to the codes' original meanings. It describes a temporary practice while new codes are being designed.
